title: Lukashenko's Moscow flight offer: a stalled channel, not a breakthrough
from: LUKASHENKO OFFERS TO FLY ZELENSKIY TO MOSCOW FOR TALKS
bottomLine: Lukashenko's offer to fly Zelensky to Moscow is a signal of Belarus and Moscow seeking a Slavic-only format that excludes Europe, not a credible path to peace; Kyiv has rejected it outright. For U.S. interests the story matters because it sits alongside a live US-brokered trilateral track, and because Belarus's own sanctions-for-prisoners channel with Washington gives Minsk leverage it can use to shape who gets a seat at the table.

summary.plain: Belarus's leader offered to fly Ukraine's president to Moscow for a meeting. Ukraine's president laughed it off and said the other leaders should come to Kyiv instead. Nobody with real power has said yes.

context.label: Right now
context.text: Lukashenko's offer to fly Zelensky to Moscow for talks with Putin was made in a Le Point interview and rejected by Zelensky on Nov 24. It comes as a trilateral US-Russia-Ukraine track has restarted after the Abu Dhabi talks of Nov 10–11.

context.label: How we got here
context.text: Minsk I and II (2014–15) were signed in Minsk under the OSCE and Normandy formats and were never fully implemented. In 2022 Belarus hosted early talks at Lyaskavichy and Kamyanyuki before the process moved to Istanbul.

context.label: The politics
context.text: Russia wants Donbas and no NATO membership; Ukraine wants a ceasefire on current lines and security guarantees. US officials say territory cannot be settled until security guarantees are agreed. Congress passed a sanctions bill in 2026 whose use remains unclear.

context.label: The people
context.text: Lukashenko wants a seat at the table and sanctions relief. Zelensky wants direct talks on neutral ground with European participation. Putin insists on Moscow and Donbas. Witkoff and Kushner run the US track and have announced a European seat that Moscow disputes.

context.label: Why now, and what's next
context.text: The offer was published Nov 24 and the full interview was due Nov 25. The next trilateral round has no confirmed date. Reported US targets of early January 2027 and a pre-Christmas push are unverified.

context.label: The culture and the public
context.text: Ukrainian public opinion is split between openness to negotiations (KIIS: 75%) and reluctance to cede territory (54% reject transferring all Donbas). Russian support for talks has slipped from 66% to 61% since December.

sections.title: The offer is rhetorical and Kyiv has rejected it
paragraphs: Lukashenko's offer was made in an interview with the French weekly Le Point, conducted by Anne Nivat and recorded on November 17. BelTA, the Belarusian state agency, released the remarks on November 24. The core line, as Reuters rendered it, was that "Volodya Zelensky and I could simply go and fly to Moscow," with Lukashenko acting as "guarantor of his safety." He also said the three Slavic states could settle matters faster without Europe, and that if Zelensky refused, "let him go to the front" with a weapon. Reuters flagged his claim that Russian forces are "winning" as his own view, not a sourced battlefield fact. Note that the "suitcase" wording attributed to Zelensky differs across translations, so verify the primary text before quoting it.

Kyiv's response was immediate and dismissive. Speaking to reporters in Berehove, Zakarpattia, on November 24, Zelensky called the idea "not a serious conversation" and said neither Moscow nor Kyiv is a viable venue while the war continues. He countered that Lukashenko should bring Putin to Kyiv, with safe reception guaranteed. Moscow has not publicly answered the proposal. Its standing line, repeated by Lavrov on October 31, is that Zelensky should come to Moscow, and Putin has said he will meet only there. The offer thus sits between two capitals that already reject each other's venues, and Minsk has no agreed role in that dispute.

The proposal lacks what a serious channel requires: a venue agreed by both sides, a date, a negotiating mandate, or a named counterpart. Lukashenko offered no timetable and no location beyond a flight to Moscow. In May he had already offered to meet Zelensky, with no meeting following. The pattern suggests the offer is a statement of position rather than an initiative that either party is preparing to act on.

The historical weight of Belarus cuts against it. Minsk hosted the 2014–15 accords and the early 2022 talks at Lyaskavichy and Kamyanyuki, but the process moved to Istanbul within weeks, and Kyiv has since treated Belarus as a party to the invasion rather than a neutral host. For a Ukrainian audience, a proposal from Lukashenko carries the weight of an ally of the invader, which explains the sharp tone of Zelensky's reply.
sections.why: the offer is best read as signalling that Minsk and Moscow want a Slavic-only format excluding Europe, not as a credible path to talks.

sections.title: Minsk's mediator role is contested and self-interested
paragraphs: Belarus's credibility as broker is weak, and the record explains why. Minsk hosted the 2014–15 Minsk I and II talks, which were signed in Minsk and are remembered in Kyiv as a frame that left Ukraine exposed. Minsk II was a political commitment rather than a treaty, and no parliament ratified it. Ukraine's then foreign minister Pavlo Klimkin called it "a way of making us fundamentally dependent" on Russia. Those agreements were brokered under a Normandy format and overseen by the OSCE. Belarus provided the room, not the referee.

The 2022 record is more damaging. Talks opened on 28 February 2022 near Lyaskavichy, with further rounds at Kamyanyuki on 3 and 7 March. Those rounds were short-lived: the process moved to Istanbul within weeks, and Belarus was never a formal participant. Its own account is that it "has never asked for the role of a mediator." Yet Belarus allowed Russian troops to use its territory as a rear base for the invasion, and Ukraine alleges that relay transmitters on the border guided drone strikes. Lukashenko has also described himself and Putin as "co-aggressors," a remark reported in October 2026 by one secondary source and not independently confirmed. A party that has been an open staging ground for the attack it is now offering to mediate cannot credibly present itself as neutral.

Kyiv will not accept a Minsk venue. Zelensky has said neither Moscow nor Kyiv is a viable setting while the war continues, and Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has reportedly said any face-to-face meeting must take place on neutral ground, not in Moscow or Belarus. Kyiv has also sanctioned Lukashenko personally, most restrictions for ten years, which makes a Minsk-hosted summit politically untenable for Zelensky before any question of security is addressed.

Moscow's interest is opportunistic. Putin has said he would meet only in Moscow, yet has also said Belarus could again provide a venue, so Minsk serves as a fallback when Moscow's own preferred format stalls. The Slavic-only framing that Lukashenko offered, with Russia, Ukraine and Belarus settling matters "without the Europeans," matches the Kremlin's objection to the European seat that Washington has announced. Belarus gains standing and possibly sanctions relief from being seen as useful; Moscow gains a format that dilutes European leverage. Neither benefit is a commitment to a settlement.
sections.why: a Minsk venue would hand Moscow a format that excludes Europe and reopens the Minsk-II model that Kyiv has spent a decade rejecting.

sections.title: A US-brokered trilateral track is the real game
paragraphs: The trilateral track now runs through Washington. The U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have shuttled between Moscow and Kyiv since the autumn. Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo and Putin in St. Petersburg in October. On Nov 3 he announced talks in Abu Dhabi, and on Nov 10–11 the three sides met there, the first trilateral round since February, when the process was suspended amid the Iran war. The session produced a large prisoner-of-war exchange and no territorial breakthrough. On Nov 12 Witkoff and Kushner spent about two and a half hours with Putin in the Kremlin, after which Witkoff said a new trilateral round had been agreed and that Europeans would join.

What has been agreed is narrow: prisoner exchanges, a channel for talks, and a shared interest in a ceasefire. What remains blocked is the core of the war. Russia demands that Ukraine cede the parts of Donetsk and Luhansk it has not taken and bar NATO membership. Ukraine wants a ceasefire on current lines. U.S. officials have said territory cannot be settled until security guarantees are agreed, and Putin has called territory "a bone of contention" while rejecting foreign peacekeepers as a "continuation of war." Ukraine has put forward narrower asks, including a Black Sea de-escalation deal and a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure before winter.

The European seat is where the Slavic-only format collides with the U.S. process. Kushner said on Nov 12 that "both sides" had agreed to widen the next round to include European partners, and Witkoff called it "a very big deal." Ushakov and Lavrov played that down, and Peskov said only that Putin "has never refused to engage with the Europeans." Putin has conditioned European involvement on Europeans first visiting Moscow. Lukashenko's proposal that the three Slavic states settle matters without Europe therefore echoes the Kremlin's objection to the format Washington has announced. Kyiv has insisted on European participation throughout, so a Belarus-centred format would give Moscow and Minsk the outcome they prefer while Washington's own design is set aside.

The process also carries history that shapes expectations in Kyiv. The 2014–15 Minsk agreements, signed under German and French facilitation, were never ratified by any parliament and were seen by Ukraine as tying it to Russia. The 2022 Istanbul talks, held after the Belarus-hosted rounds, broke down over Bucha and Donbas demands, and each side blames the other. Ukrainian polling from September 2026 shows 75% open to negotiations, but KIIS stresses this is not support for territorial concessions. That gap limits how much room any negotiator has.
sections.why: the next trilateral round, its date and whether Europe sits at the table will decide whether Washington's track remains the main channel or gives way to a Minsk-centred format Kyiv has already rejected.

sections.title: Washington's Belarus channel gives Minsk leverage
paragraphs: Washington's channel to Minsk runs through a single envoy, John Coale, and it trades sanctions relief for prisoner releases. In March 2026, 250 prisoners were freed in exchange for relief on two state banks, the Finance Ministry and potash producers. On September 16, 2026, 25 were freed in return for delisting Lakokraska and Bellesbumprom, an outcome described as an "interim deal." The drop from 250 to 25 is itself a signal: the currency Minsk receives has shrunk, and it knows Washington wants more.

That gives Lukashenko leverage well beyond the prisoners themselves. Each release buys him a seat in the room with a U.S. official, a reason for Washington to keep sanctions on the table without pressing harder, and a claim that he is useful to American diplomacy. Coale has also promised to press U.S. banks to return tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets, a concrete benefit the regime can point to at home. A government that is still under EU sanctions, which were extended to February 28, 2027, and that is accused by Kyiv of letting Russian forces use its territory, is being rewarded for transactional cooperation.

The human-rights cost is real. Viasna counts more than 900 political prisoners still held, and Tsikhanouskaya and Viasna describe the releases as bargaining chips, not reforms. Lukashenko denies that Belarus holds political prisoners at all, which means each release is presented domestically as a favour rather than a correction. Trading sanctions relief for a few dozen people risks normalising the practice of holding prisoners as currency, and it gives Minsk little reason to stop taking people in the first place. Advocates for the prisoners have no comparable lever in the room.

The larger problem is that Washington has no stated position on Belarus as a venue. Lukashenko's offer to host or fly the parties to Moscow lands on a channel where the U.S. has been negotiating with Minsk on prisoners but has not said whether Belarus should have any role in the peace process. I found no White House comment on the Lukashenko offer, and no U.S. statement endorsing or ruling out a Minsk format. Coale's "return in about a month" was not confirmed in the results reviewed, so even the cadence of this channel is unclear. Silence lets Minsk read Washington's engagement as an endorsement of its standing.
sections.why: unless Washington separates the prisoner track from any question of Belarusian mediation, the regime will treat its sanctions bargaining as a credential for a seat at the table it was never invited to.

sections.title: Implications for U.S. interests and realistic options
paragraphs: Washington faces three linked decisions. The first is whether to accept or reject Belarus as a venue. Kyiv has already ruled out Minsk and Moscow, and Washington has not endorsed any Belarusian role. Minsk hosted the 2014–15 Minsk talks and the early 2022 rounds at Lyaskavichy and Kamyanyuki, but Istanbul took over within weeks, and the Minsk II framework was never ratified by any parliament and failed on the battlefield balance. Those precedents argue against a Belarusian venue now. Rejecting Minsk outright is the cleaner position, and it costs little, since Moscow's interest in the format is opportunistic and Lukashenko's own line on mediation is inconsistent.

The second decision is how to balance prisoner deals against sanctions. Envoy John Coale's track has freed 250 prisoners in March 2026 and 25 in September, in exchange for relief on state banks, the Finance Ministry, potash producers and two firms. Viasna still counts more than 900 political prisoners. Each deal rewards Minsk with leverage in Washington while the releases remain small relative to the total held. Washington should keep any further relief tied to verified releases of named prisoners, with a fixed schedule, and stop trading sanctions for headline numbers. Relief should not reach the state entities that finance the war, and Washington should make clear to Minsk that it has no role in the trilateral settlement.

The third is keeping European participation. Witkoff and Kushner announced after the Nov 12 Kremlin meeting that Europeans would join the next round, and Lukashenko's Slavic-only format directly contradicts it. Washington should hold that European seat as a condition of any new round, because Europe controls the sanctions architecture Russia will need relief from and the security guarantees Kyiv says it needs before territory can be settled. The main risk of this course is that Moscow refuses the European format and the track stalls, leaving Washington with a process that looks like it is waiting on the Kremlin. The alternative risk is accepting a Minsk-linked format to keep Moscow at the table, which would discredit the process in Kyiv and in Europe and reward Belarus for its role in the invasion.

Timing sharpens these choices. Reported US hopes for a deal before Christmas or by early January 2027 rest on a single unverified source, and the core dispute over Donbas remains unresolved. Pressing for a fast leaders' summit before territory and guarantees are settled would likely produce a thin deal that Kyiv cannot accept. A realistic near-term aim is to consolidate the technical Abu Dhabi track, expand prisoner exchanges and keep a truce on energy infrastructure in view. Washington should weigh that against the domestic calendar and the Graham sanctions act, whose implementation is unconfirmed.

The recommended course is to reject Minsk as a venue, keep the European seat in any trilateral format, and tie further Belarus relief strictly to verified prisoner releases. The risk is that Moscow treats the refusal as a reason to slow the track, and that Lukashenko uses his remaining US channel to press for relief regardless.
sections.why: a Belarus venue would hand Minsk a seat it has not earned, and a Slavic-only format would quietly drop the Europeans whose sanctions and guarantees any durable settlement depends on.

people.name: Jared Corey Kushner
people.role: U.S. SPECIAL ENVOY (INFORMAL, VOLUNTEER) ON UKRAINE AND MIDDLE EAST NEGOTIATIONS; FOUNDER AND OWNER OF AFFINITY PARTNERS
people.lede: Kushner co-leads the U.S. track with Steve Witkoff, having pressed Moscow and Kyiv to add European participation to the next round and pushing for a deal by early 2027. Lukashenko's Moscow-flight offer sits outside the format Kushner has publicly announced, which includes Europe.

blocks.heading: Who they are
blocks.text: Jared Kushner is Donald Trump's son-in-law and a New York real-estate investor turned private investor who now serves as one of the administration's main envoys. He has no formal government title, which his critics say lets him avoid financial disclosure, while his supporters point to his access to Trump as the reason he is trusted to negotiate. In the Ukraine file he works alongside Witkoff, and in the Middle East he has been a central figure since 2025. He also runs Affinity Partners, a Miami investment firm whose capital comes largely from Gulf sovereign funds.

blocks.heading: Personality and style
blocks.text: Kushner's own statements show a preference for framing progress and for pressing Kyiv to keep talks private. An interview he gave to New York Magazine reports that he criticized Kyiv's public discussion of the negotiations as counterproductive, and that he tried to keep Trump from pressuring Zelensky. A U.S. official described him to RFE/RL as someone who 'does not make statements without thought or understanding of all the parties involved,' while critics such as Ukrainian commentators have questioned whether his public claims about Russian positions match Moscow's own statements.

blocks.heading: Career highlights
items: 1981: Born in Livingston, New Jersey; Harvard B.A. in government with honors in 2003 and NYU JD/MBA in 2007.
2005: Took over the family real-estate business Kushner Companies after his father's conviction on 18 criminal charges; the father served until 2006.
2007-2008: Led Kushner Companies' purchase of 666 Fifth Avenue for a record $1.8 billion, later needing partners after the 2008 crash.
2017-2021: Senior adviser to Trump and director of the Office of American Innovation; led the First Step Act and the Middle East peace effort behind the Abraham Accords.
2021: Founded Affinity Partners, which received a $2 billion investment from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.
2025-2026: Returned as an informal envoy on Gaza and Ukraine; formally described in some reporting as a special envoy for peace in 2026.

blocks.heading: Current involvements
items: Informal U.S. envoy on Ukraine talks with Steve Witkoff: the Abu Dhabi trilateral round, the Moscow and Dublin meetings of Nov. 12-13, and Berlin talks with Coalition of the Willing members on Nov. 19.
Publicly pushing a 'common understanding' on European security architecture 'over the coming weeks,' which conflicts with European leaders who want a ceasefire first, according to Euronews.
Pending work on a prisoner exchange described by Kushner as the largest of the war; he said in November that details would be announced 'shortly.'

Floated Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine, which he says Trump would have to approve subject to constitutional and congressional processes; Moscow has publicly rejected any arrangement amounting to quasi-membership in NATO.
Affinity Partners remains active, with the firm reporting about $6.2 billion in assets at the end of 2025 and retaining its largest-shareholder stake in Israel's Phoenix Financial.
Democratic oversight: House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia requested Affinity's Middle East fundraising and investment records in October 2026.

blocks.heading: Big wins
items: Helped broker the Abraham Accords and related Israel-Arab normalization deals in 2020, as described in his biographical record.
Helped restart trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, the first since February, which produced an agreed prisoner exchange.
Secured Russia's stated agreement, as he presented it, to European participation in the next round, a point Kremlin spokesman Peskov has not confirmed.
Affinity's Phoenix Financial stake returned more than five times its cost in July 2026, according to CNN and Calcalist reporting.

blocks.heading: Controversies
items: CNN reported in October 2026 that Affinity Partners is the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial, which invests in Israeli arms makers including Elbit Systems; Kushner's attorney said he has 'never participated in or directed Phoenix's decisions.'

House Oversight Democrats led by Robert Garcia said in October 2026 that Kushner's dual role as envoy and investor presents 'significant conflicts of interest,' and that he avoids disclosure to Congress; Kushner's side did not respond to the request.

Affinity's raising of capital from Saudi, Emirati and Qatari sovereign funds while Kushner negotiated in the Middle East has drawn criticism from Democrats and commentators, who say the arrangement blurs commercial and diplomatic interests.
A November 2026 amended SEC filing added $34 million of defense-supplier shares (Arxis) that were absent from the original report; the filings do not say who made the decision.

blocks.heading: Who they align with
items: Patron: Donald Trump, his father-in-law, who has backed his envoy role and reportedly said he trusts Kushner to negotiate.
Ally: Steve Witkoff, co-lead on the U.S. Russia and Ukraine track and co-author of the trilateral format.
Backers: Saudi Public Investment Fund, plus sovereign funds from the UAE and Qatar, which have financed Affinity Partners.

Counterpart in Europe: Coalition of the Willing leaders, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, who have pressed for European seats and for revisiting Ukraine's NATO path.
Rival: Kremlin aides Yuri Ushakov, Sergei Ryabkov and Sergei Lavrov, who have played down or rejected a European seat and NATO-linked guarantees.
Rival: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who has publicly clashed with Kushner over whether security architecture should be negotiated before a ceasefire.
Rival: House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, who is investigating his investments and dual role.
